S&P 500 is on track for its first 6-day losing streak since April 2024, down another 1.9% currently.

▪️ The index is down 5.8% over the six sessions (November 12–19), worse than the 4.5% drop in the April 12–19, 2024 streak.
▪️ There were three 5-day losing streaks in between: Dec. 26, 2024–Jan. 2, 2025 (−2.8%), August 15–21, 2025 (−1.5%) and June 22–26, 2026 (−2.0%). None of them made it to six.
▪️ The index is now 8.2% below its October 6 record close. At these levels it would be the lowest close since April 29.

The silver lining is that all four of those earlier streaks (the April 2024 six-day run and the three five-day runs) bounced the next session. The index was higher a month later each time, by 1.0% to 6.9%. 

The April 2024 streak ended right at that pullback’s low, and the index was up 6.9% a month later. But four cases is a tiny sample, and none of those streaks did this much damage.

With Anthropic ($ANT) set to begin trading today, a look at how 16 big, high-profile US IPOs since 2008 did over their first year.

From the first-day close:

▪ The median was down 29% after 12 months, and the average was down 14%.
▪ Only 4 of 16 were higher, and just 3 beat the S&P 500, which gained a median 11% over the same windows.
▪ The winners were Arm (+118%), CoreWeave (+94%), Snowflake (+27%) and Airbnb (+25%). 
▪ The losers included Robinhood (−74%), Rivian (−67%), Lyft (−66%) and Coupang (−62%).

Even from the IPO price, the median was −18%, despite a median first-day pop of +27%.

Note, though, that most of the median underperformance came in months 3 - 12.

Continuing claims jump but mostly due to Michigan per Goldman:

Initial jobless claims come in at 203,000 for the week ending November 14, above the 198,000 estimate and up 1,000 from an upwardly revised 202,000, the highest since September 5. The four-week average rose 2,000 to 197,750, the highest since October 17, but remains close to the 195,250 two weeks earlier that was the lowest since October 1969.

Continuing claims jumped 70,000, the most since January 2024, to 1,763,000, the highest since August 29, well above the 1,703,000 estimate. That came after the prior week was revised down to 1,693,000, the lowest since March 2023. Their four-week average is 235,500 lower year-over-year, down for a 42nd straight week, though the gap narrowed from the prior week’s 245,250, the largest since December 2022.

On the spike in continuing claims from Goldman: "Much of the increase is driven by Michigan, where continuing claims increased by 44k and initial claims increased by 7k, both the largest increases since the pandemic. We suspect that this spike is related to the launch of Michigan’s new unemployment insurance platform and does not mark a genuine softening in the labor market."

Headline: AAII Bears Retreat Even as Stocks Slide

Bearishness in the AAII sentiment survey eased to 42.2% this week from 51.4% last week, when it topped 50% for the first time in eight weeks. Bullishness edged up to 33.3% from 30.8%, and neutral sentiment jumped to 24.4% from 17.8%.

That narrowed the bull-bear spread to −8.9 from −20.6 and lifted the bull/bear ratio to 0.79 from 0.60, though it remains below its 1.18 long-run average, with bears still well above their 31.5% historical average and bulls below their 37.5%.

What stands out is the timing. Retail investors got less bearish over a stretch in which the S&P 500 fell 3.5% (Thursday to Wednesday, the survey period) and closed below its November 5th low.

Last week’s spread below −20 was the kind of reading DB notes has typically been followed by gains (S&P higher a month later 68% of the time, median +2.8%, since 2010), so some of that contrarian cushion has now been used up.

Headline: AAII Bears Retreat Even as Stocks Slide

Bearishness in the AAII sentiment survey eased to 42.2% this week from 51.4% last week, when it topped 50% for the first time in eight weeks. Bullishness edged up to 33.3% from 30.8%, and neutral sentiment jumped to 24.4% from 17.8%.

That narrowed the bull-bear spread to −8.9 from −20.6 and lifted the bull/bear ratio to 0.79 from 0.60, though it remains below its 1.18 long-run average, with bears still well above their 31.5% historical average and bulls below their 37.5%.

What stands out is the timing. Retail investors got less bearish over a stretch in which the S&P 500 fell 3.5% (Thursday to Wednesday, the survey period) and closed below its November 5th low.

Last week’s spread below −20 was the kind of reading DB notes has typically been followed by gains (S&P higher a month later 68% of the time, median +2.8%, since 2010), so some of that contrarian cushion has now been used up.

Goldman: Everyone around the Thanksgiving table by now has probably heard how positive seasonality is in the November-December period. If this tape has taught us anything, it is that we need to zoom in far more closely than a 2-month period. In fact, there is a clear “holiday” ramp up. 

Performance has historically received a boost in the immediate Thanksgiving period, stalled out in early December, only to be reignited once again in the next round of holiday cheer. Whether this plays out exactly is of course unknown, but it is a factor to be aware of.

The caveat: Looking back to 1990, in the 17 years when VIX started mid-November at 18 or higher, as it does now, it was lower by year-end in 14, by -3.25 pts on average. In those same years SPX's year-end gain was smaller (mean +1.34%, up in 59% of years). 

As outlined above, the period usually sees a dip first – the median drawdown within the window is -3.0%. Additionally, most of the gains come late; from Dec 15th to year-end the mean is +1.22%, and SPX rose in 27 of 36 years

I had flagged in the Week Ahead the softening in the McClellan Summation Index but noted it had not hit the 100 point level that has historically been significant. 

Well, it has now well surpassed that falling 131 points on Wednesday alone, after drops of 72 points Monday and 138 Tuesday, leaving it 350 points below its November 12th peak of 260.65. That peak came 25 sessions after the October 8th sub-zero turn, in line with the 26-session median for the first rollover after the 12 prior sub-zero turns since 2018. What’s unusual, as I noted in the Week Ahead, is how little it rose first: about 1,450 points, which ranks with December 2021 (about 1,470) and October 2018 (about 1,060) as the smallest of the 13, and about half the roughly 2,900-point median.

Six of the prior turns rolled over after rises of less than 3,000 points, and in five of them (all but March 2023) the NYSE closed below its pre-turn low within three months, by a median of about 9% at its worst close. 

In each of those five, the Summation was back below zero within seven weeks of its peak (October 2018 never got above it), while in March 2023, the one that held, it stayed positive for more than five months. This time it took just four sessions, matching May 2022, when the NYSE had broken its pre-turn low a session earlier. 

The NYSE has fallen 3.9% in three sessions and closed Wednesday just 0.3% above its September 30th low (23,490.80), so a close below that level would be the confirmation.

The @dailychartbook nightly email had an interesting post about the VIX. @McClellanOsc (via @LJKawa) notes that spot VIX has moved above all of its futures contracts, a “fairly rare condition” tied to “a bottoming condition for prices.” His caveat is that it’s not necessarily “the exact moment of the bottom.”

Cboe data back to late 2007 show spot VIX closing above 3-month VIX (VIX3M) is relatively rare, happening on about 10% of trading days in 75 separate episodes. On Tuesday spot VIX also closed above 6-month VIX (25.46 vs. 25.37), which fits McClellan’s read.

The good news is returns have been a bit better than average right away, and better still once the curve flips back. Median S&P 500 return one and three months later (share of cases higher in parentheses):

▪️ All days: +1.5% (66%) and +3.8% (73%).
▪️ First day of inversion: +2.5% (71%) and +4.4% (71%).
▪️ Day the curve flips back: +3.2% (81%) and +5.4% (79%).

Why not buy right away then? The inversions that drag on are the problem. The 21 episodes that lasted more than a week (2008, 2011, late 2018 and 2020 among them) saw a median −0.8% the next month, with only 48% higher. Since you only know how long one lasts after the fact, waiting for the curve to flip back may be worthwhile.

This month is a case study. On Nov. 5 the VIX jumped from 16.6 to 28.2, putting it 10% above VIX3M. The curve flipped back on Nov. 9, and the S&P rallied 3.6% by Nov. 11. Then it rolled over to close at 7,324 on Wednesday, its lowest close since July 29 and 6.3% below the Oct. 6 record. As of Wednesday’s close, VIX/VIX3M is 1.01, a shallow two-day inversion.

Nomura’s Charlie McElligott adds a wrinkle in another post in the same email. He says aggregate S&P dealer gamma has fallen to −$7.3B, the deepest on Nomura’s chart going back to 2019, meaning “dealers are now selling into every dip and buying into every rip.” That can make inversions come and go quickly, so a single flip back is a weak all-clear.

Bottom line: The inversion says we’re in the zone where lows tend to form. The more useful tell is a flip back that sticks. If the curve stays inverted, this starts to look more like late 2018 or 2020 than a quick dip.

Cboe data back to late 2007 show spot VIX closing above 3-month VIX (VIX3M) is relatively rare, happening on about 10% of trading days in 75 separate episodes. On Tuesday spot VIX also closed above 6-month VIX (25.46 vs. 25.37), which fits McClellan’s read.

The good news is returns have been a bit better than average right away, and better still once the curve flips back. Median S&P 500 return one and three months later (share of cases higher in parentheses):

▪️ All days: +1.5% (66%) and +3.8% (73%).
▪️ First day of inversion: +2.5% (71%) and +4.4% (71%).
▪️ Day the curve flips back: +3.2% (81%) and +5.4% (79%).

Why not buy right away then? The inversions that drag on are the problem. The 21 episodes that lasted more than a week (2008, 2011, late 2018 and 2020 among them) saw a median −0.8% the next month, with only 48% higher. Since you only know how long one lasts after the fact, waiting for the curve to flip back may be worthwhile.

This month is a case study. On Nov. 5 the VIX jumped from 16.6 to 28.2, putting it 10% above VIX3M. The curve flipped back on Nov. 9, and the S&P rallied 3.6% by Nov. 11. Then it rolled over to close at 7,324 on Wednesday, its lowest close since July 29 and 6.3% below the Oct. 6 record. As of Wednesday’s close, VIX/VIX3M is 1.01, a shallow two-day inversion.

Nomura’s Charlie McElligott adds a wrinkle in another post in the same email. He says aggregate S&P dealer gamma has fallen to −$7.3B, the deepest on Nomura’s chart going back to 2019, meaning “dealers are now selling into every dip and buying into every rip.” That can make inversions come and go quickly, so a single flip back is a weak all-clear.

Bottom line: The inversion says we’re in the zone where lows tend to form. The more useful tell is a flip back that sticks. If the curve stays inverted, this starts to look more like late 2018 or 2020 than a quick dip.

$TTWO Take-Two heads into today's GTA VI launch stronger than for any earlier main Grand Theft Auto game:
▪ It beat the S&P 500 by 9.1 points over the last 30 trading days (about 12 including after-hours). The prior six launches had a median of −4.9, and only GTA 2 (1999) was also positive.
▪ Wed's +6.2% (S&P −0.2%) is its biggest day-before-launch gain of the series. The prior six ranged from −8.1% to +5.3%.
▪ Launch day has historically been modest: 4 of 6 beat the S&P, with a median of +1 point. GTA V and San Andreas both lagged.
▪ Thirty days after launch, the median gain over the S&P is +3 points. In the four launches since 2002 it has been flat, from −0.9 to +5.4.

Historically the stock gained well before the release and faded into launch. This time it’s rallying right into it.
